title: What Happens to the Secrets You Share With AI Chatbots
excerpt: Proton's new AI Paper Trail tool reveals how much ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini know about their users — and most people never think to check.
body:
• Proton has launched AI Paper Trail, a free tool that analyzes exported data from ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to show users exactly what these platforms have inferred about them.
  • Major AI companies collect and retain chat data by default, using it to train models — opt-out settings exist but are buried in menus and not enabled by default.
  • Even with training opt-outs enabled, AI providers retain conversation logs for 30 days or more for safety monitoring, and some share conversations with human reviewers.
  • Privacy-first alternatives like Proton's Lumo use zero-access encryption and open-source models, keeping no server-side logs of conversations.

Proton, the Swiss company behind encrypted email and VPN services, has released a free tool called AI Paper Trail that lets users see exactly what major AI chatbots have learned about them. The tool analyzes exported data from OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, and Google's Gemini to reveal the extent of user profiling and data retention across these platforms.

What AI Chatbots Know About You

Every time a user types a prompt into an AI chatbot, that information is likely being used to further train the underlying large language model. AI companies collect data from conversations to improve their models — and the scope of what they retain goes far beyond what most users realize.

According to Fast Company, the data users provide becomes part of the model itself. Health concerns, financial details, relationship troubles, and workplace frustrations shared in casual conversation with a chatbot can all become training data. "The chatbot may give you the answers you're searching for, but it will also use all the data you give it to further train its models — and retain that data as part of itself," Fast Company reported.

AI companies say they anonymize information before using it for training, but users must take their word for it. Even anonymized data carries risks — a bad actor could potentially link prompts about specific health, legal, or financial issues back to an individual user.

The Opt-Out Problem

The four most popular chatbots — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Perplexity — all offer ways to opt out of data training. In ChatGPT, users must navigate to Settings, then Data Controls, and toggle off "Improve the model for everyone." Claude requires accessing the privacy menu and toggling off "Help improve Claude." Google's Gemini requires visiting a separate Gemini Apps Activity settings page to turn off data collection.

The catch: none of these settings are enabled by default. Users who skip them "effectively send their data into a black box," according to Fast Company. Google will even show a subset of conversations to human reviewers without disclosing when that happens. ChatGPT's "Temporary Chat" mode, designed to avoid storing conversation history, still retains conversations for up to 30 days for safety reasons.

"Before we created Lumo, I'd use ChatGPT sometimes. But then I'd feel really dirty after using it, because who the hell knows what Sam [Altman] is going to do with all my data?"

— Andy Yen, Proton CEO

How AI Paper Trail Works

Proton's AI Paper Trail tool lets users export their data from major AI platforms and then analyzes it to reveal what these services have inferred. The tool surfaces the extent of user profiling and data retention practices that are otherwise invisible to users, positioning it as a transparency mechanism for an industry that operates largely as a black box.

The release comes alongside Proton's own AI chatbot, Lumo, which the company pitches as a privacy-first alternative. Lumo uses open-source models from companies like Mistral and Nvidia, running on Proton's European data centers. The chatbot uses zero-access encryption — the same technology behind Proton Mail — so conversations are decrypted only on users' devices. Proton says it keeps no server-side logs of conversations.

According to TechCrunch, Lumo 2.0 added image generation, memory features, and private web search while maintaining its no-log, no-training-data architecture. The chatbot includes a "Ghost mode" that permanently deletes conversations when users close the window.

Workplace Risks

The privacy implications extend beyond personal use. Employees using AI chatbots for work could inadvertently expose their employers to legal and regulatory risks. Proprietary code, sales data, and confidential client information entered into chatbots can become part of the model's training data. Several multinational companies have already banned ChatGPT internally, according to Proton's engineering director Eamonn Maguire, because they "can't risk their data disappearing into a black box."

DuckDuckGo offers a partial solution through Duck.ai, which proxies queries to OpenAI and Anthropic while stripping personal information. Apple Intelligence similarly routes requests through privacy-preserving infrastructure. But these intermediaries still rely on major AI providers' servers to process queries.

What Diaspora Tech Workers Should Know

For Indian-origin tech professionals in the US — many of whom work at companies building or deploying AI systems — the privacy calculus is particularly relevant. Sharing immigration paperwork, visa details, or financial planning information with AI chatbots could create data trails that are difficult to control or delete. The practical advice from security researchers: disable training toggles on every chatbot you use, redact sensitive information before uploading documents, and consider privacy-first alternatives for conversations involving personal or professional details.
